lesson.title: Clipping: Running Out of Voltage Mid-Wave
lesson.summary: Clipping happens when a signal's required voltage swing exceeds what an amplifier's power supply rails can deliver, flattening the peaks of the waveform and generating a sudden burst of harsh, high order harmonic distortion.
lesson.body:
Every amplifying stage runs from a power supply with finite voltage rails. As you already know from op-amp saturation, even a stage that behaves ideally across most of its range can only swing its output up to somewhere near its supply rail voltages, usually a bit less than the rails themselves because of internal losses in the output stage. If the input signal, combined with the circuit's gain, calls for an output swing larger than the rails can actually deliver, the top and bottom of the waveform simply cannot go any higher or lower. They flatten off at whatever the maximum available voltage happens to be, chopping the peaks off the wave. That flat topped shape is clipping.

Clipping is a severe, abrupt form of nonlinearity, so by the same mechanism described in the harmonic distortion chapter, it generates a large burst of harmonics all at once. Because clipping typically affects the positive and negative halves of a sine wave symmetrically, the resulting distortion is dominated by odd order harmonics, the third, fifth, seventh, and so on, which tend to sound especially harsh and buzzy compared to the smoother, less aggressive harmonic content produced by milder forms of overload.

Here is a worked example. An op-amp stage runs from plus and minus 15 V supply rails. Due to realistic saturation losses in its output stage, roughly 1.5 V near each rail, it can only actually swing to about plus and minus 13.5 V, since 15 minus 1.5 equals 13.5. Now suppose the gain stage is driven hard enough that, in order to reproduce the input signal faithfully, it would need to swing all the way to plus and minus 18 V at its peaks. Since only 13.5 V is actually available, the fraction of the intended peak the waveform actually reaches is 13.5 divided by 18, which equals exactly 0.75. In other words, the waveform reaches only 75 percent of its intended peak voltage before it runs out of room, and the top 25 percent of each half cycle's swing is simply cut off flat.

Not all clipping looks the same. Soft clipping rounds off gradually as a circuit approaches its limit, a behavior common in tube stages and some transistor designs, while hard clipping produces an abrupt, sharp flat top, common in op-amps and in digital systems hitting full scale. Both are still clipping by the definition above, but soft clipping tends to generate comparatively lower order, less harsh sounding harmonics than an abrupt hard clip. This is exactly why headroom, covered earlier in this sequence, exists in the first place: it is the deliberately built in margin meant to keep ordinary signal peaks safely below this clipping point.
